strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and underexplored problem: detecting misleading creator intent in multimodal news, moving beyond surface-level cross-modal misalignment
High-quality dataset construction with rigorous filtering, systematic intent-guided generation, and strong human validation (99.2% accuracy, κ=0.877 for text)
Comprehensive evaluation of 14 state-of-the-art VLMs across three related tasks with both implication-oriented and consistency-oriented reasoning approaches
Insightful multi-faceted analysis revealing how VLMs rely on spurious cues (cross-modal consistency, stylistic signals, authenticity hints) rather than genuine intent understanding
Clear presentation with effective visualizations, complete appendices supporting reproducibility, and responsible disclosure plans
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: primarily a benchmark paper leveraging existing tools (GPT-4o, FLUX) with straightforward prompting-based evaluation; no new detection methods or solutions proposed
Synthetic data representativeness concerns: entire 12,000-instance dataset generated by LLMs; human validation only covers 2% of data; potential data leakage or model-specific artifacts not analyzed

Fuzzy task definitions: 'misleading' is subjective; Creator Desire Inference achieves poor performance (0-75.2% F1) with some models at 0%, but paper doesn't adequately discuss whether the task is well-posed

Insufficient statistical rigor: no confidence intervals, error bars, or significance testing; models run once with temperature=0; limited baselines including no human performance; key analyses use small sample sizes (200 samples for image generation)

Limited practical impact: no solutions proposed for identified problems; evaluation assumes trustworthy reference articles available, unrealistic in real-world deployment; benchmark limited to English, Western-centric news from VisualNews
Reference article dependency: evaluation setup assumes ground-truth context always available, contradicting real-world MMD scenarios where trusted references are rarely accessible
Moderate inter-annotator agreement for images (κ=0.703) and human validation limited to 2% of dataset raises questions about label quality at scale
No fine-tuning experiments: only prompt-based evaluation; no investigation of how models could be adapted for this task

strengths: Novel problem framing: Focuses on misleading creator intent rather than surface-level misalignment, addressing an important yet underexplored aspect of multimodal misinformation detection grounded in communication theory

Exceptionally thorough human validation: 99.2% accuracy for text, 89.2% for images with high inter-annotator agreement; additional validation of data realism (98%+), and intent alignment (92%+) goes beyond typical dataset work

Comprehensive benchmark design: 12,000 samples grounded in trustworthy reference articles across 10 domains, with both text and image manipulations at multiple severity levels supporting three complementary tasks

Extensive empirical evaluation: 14 diverse VLMs evaluated with two reasoning paradigms; insightful failure analysis reveals model reliance on surface-level cues (semantic consistency, stylistic polish, spurious authenticity hints) rather than genuine intent reasoning
Demonstrated generalization: Fine-tuning on DECEPTIONDECODED transfers improvements to external MMD benchmark (MMFakeBench), suggesting utility beyond specific benchmark tasks
Strong reproducibility: Detailed appendices with prompts, model cards, evaluation protocols; reasonable ethical stance on withholding generation prompts while releasing data
weaknesses: Synthetic data with potential circularity and generalization concerns: All content generated by GPT-4o, with ground truth intent derived from the same models used to generate content. Unclear if findings generalize to real misinformation campaigns or different synthesis methods. No analysis of distribution shift from authentic misinformation.

Narrow scope limiting applicability: Restricted to subtle caption/image manipulations within single-event contexts. Excludes identifiable individuals (common in real-world misinformation) and other important types (deepfakes, multi-event composites, sequential manipulation). Claims of generality are overstated.

Task design relies on simulated intent: Ground truth intent labels from GPT-4o simulation rather than actual creators. While human validation confirms consistency, indirect validation of 'simulated intent = true creator intent' is questionable. Creates potential circularity where VLMs struggle with GPT-generated intent.

Practical applicability concerns: Consistency-oriented approach (better performing) requires trustworthy reference articles, unavailable in real deployments. Performance drops substantially without context (Table 4). Benchmark assumes idealized information environment not reflective of real-world scenarios.

Missing human performance baseline: No human accuracy reported on these tasks. Without baseline, unclear whether modest model performance (84-86% intent detection, 75% desire inference F1) represents genuine difficulty or task design issues. Prevents assessment of room for improvement.

Creator desire inference task underdeveloped: Much lower F1 scores than intent detection (Table 3), many categories with zero/near-zero performance, 8-category taxonomy not justified. Task feels hastily designed and like an afterthought rather than core contribution.

Statistical rigor gaps: No confidence intervals, significance tests, or variance analysis. Single evaluation run (temperature=0). Fine-tuning experiments on only 2 models. No error analysis by domain/topic. Missing ablations on component importance (desired influence vs. execution plan).

Incomplete analysis of failures: Limited investigation of why smaller models hallucinate, which manipulations are most deceptive, or why desire inference fails. No breakdown of performance across the 8 influence categories or by topic domain.

strengths: Novel focus on creator intent as central to multimodal misinformation detection, grounded in communication strategy theory
Rigorously constructed 12,000-sample benchmark with high-quality human validation (99.2% accuracy for text labeling, κ=0.877)
Comprehensive evaluation of 14 representative VLMs with insightful failure analysis revealing reliance on shallow cues (semantic consistency, stylistic polish)
Well-designed partial modality experiments (Table 4) and adversarial tests (spurious authenticity hints, style reframing) that expose model vulnerabilities
Demonstrated transfer learning value: fine-tuning on DECEPTIONDECODED improves performance on external MMFakeBench benchmark (7.96-30.70% gains)
Excellent documentation and reproducibility: detailed appendices with prompts, protocols, model cards, and ethics considerations
Clear and compelling presentation with well-motivated examples (Figure 1-2) and systematic evaluation design
weaknesses: Entire dataset is synthetically generated via LLMs and image generation models; no evaluation on naturally occurring misinformation limits generalization claims and real-world applicability

Creator desire inference task shows critically poor performance (0-3% F1 for many models) with minimal error analysis, suggesting either task formulation is problematic or multimodal intent reasoning is much harder than framed
Limited external validation: transfer experiments on only MMFakeBench (1,000 samples); no evaluation on PolitiFact, GossipCop, or other established benchmarks
Statistical rigor concerns: single evaluation run (temperature=0), no confidence intervals or significance testing, human validation on only 2% of data

Consistency-oriented evaluation approach provides strong task guidance (check consistency against reference article), potentially inflating performance compared to realistic unconstrained deployment scenarios
Hallucination issues in source attribution (Table 2 red cells): models sometimes predict misleading source despite non-misleading classification; limited discussion of implications
Missing analyses: no breakdown of which manipulation types are hardest to detect, limited exploration of subtle vs. significant distinction efficacy, no domain-specific performance analysis
Fine-tuning experiments limited to 2 models; unclear whether gains generalize across different architectures; potential bias from using GPT-4o for both data generation and baseline evaluation
